A town is 10 km from a spring in the hills. Design an {{< vocab "aqueduct" zh=true >}} that brings the water to the town, **with no pumps**: only gravity.

![](images/aqueduct-slope.svg){fig-alt="An aqueduct bridge carrying water on a gentle downhill slope" width="80%"}

## 1. Plan

☐ The water channel goes **downhill the whole way**, gently\
☐ Where the land dips (a valley), the channel goes over **arches**\
☐ Where a hill is in the way, the channel goes **through a tunnel** or around it\
☐ The channel is **covered**, to keep the water clean

## 2. Sketch your aqueduct

Draw the spring, the town, and your aqueduct between them. Label: **spring**, **channel**, **arches**, **town**, and the **slope**.

{{< drawing-box label="Side view: spring on the left, town on the right" >}}

{{< pagebreak >}}

## 3. {{< vocab "explain" text="Explain" zh=true >}}

**a.** {{< vocab "explain" text="Explain" zh=true >}} why the channel must slope down *gently*, not steeply.

{{< lines 3 >}}

**b.** {{< vocab "explain" text="Explain" zh=true >}} why Romans built arches instead of a solid wall across a valley. (Think: stone, weight, water from rain.)

{{< lines 3 >}}

**c.** {{< vocab "identify" text="Identify" zh=true >}} one thing a Roman city used aqueduct water for.

{{< lines 2 >}}

::: {.content-visible when-profile="teacher"}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer key"}
**a.** Too steep and the water rushes, wears away the channel and can overflow; Roman channels often dropped only a few meters over many kilometers. **b.** Arches use much less stone, are lighter, and let rivers, rain and people pass underneath. **c.** Public baths, fountains, toilets, homes, farms, mills.
:::
:::
